notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes for Exodus 12:27–51, drawn from the sources I was able to search and read.

---

## Exodus 12:27–51 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 27 — The Passover Explanation and Worship

- **Traditional Reading:** The Hebrew phrase is literally “a passover-sacrifice to Jehovah.” The emphasis falls on the word “Passover,” whose meaning was to be explained to future generations. The explanation would involve recounting the whole history of the institution, which naturally evokes gratitude and devotion. (Ellicott) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm
- The people “bowed the head and worshipped” *before* the deliverance happened — a response of faith to God’s promise. (Enduring Word / Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/
- This verse connects to the larger purpose of Passover as a teaching ordinance: parents explaining to children what God has done (cf. vv. 24–27a).

---

### v. 28 — Obedience of the People

- **Traditional Reading:** Guzik calls these “the most important words of the whole account” — the people’s deliverance depended on actually doing what God commanded. Intellectual agreement with God’s word was not enough; they had to act. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/
- Raises the provocative question: did any Israelite suffer the plague because they failed to believe and obey? Did any Egyptian who believed and applied blood get spared? (Enduring Word)

---

### v. 29 — The Tenth Plague: Death of the Firstborn at Midnight

- **Traditional Reading:** God struck “at midnight” — the weirdest, most silent, darkest hour. The plague fell on every social level, “from the firstborn of Pharaoh … to the firstborn of the captive in the dungeon.” Ellicott notes the Hebrew word for firstborn applies only to males. (Ellicott) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm
- The “dungeon” is literally “the pit-house” — pits were common prisons in Egypt. The contrast is between the highest (Pharaoh’s heir) and the lowest (a prisoner of war). (Enduring Word, citing Cole)
- **Theological Note (Reformed/Evangelical):** This plague was directed against two Egyptian gods: Osiris (giver of life) and the supposed deity of Pharaoh himself, whose own household was touched. God was executing judgment “against all the gods of Egypt” (cf. v. 12). (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/
- **Agency:** Ellicott notes that while God is said to have struck the firstborn (Ex 12:29), Exodus 12:23 attributes the work to “the destroyer,” indicating angelic agency. This does not preclude a natural agency (e.g., pestilence), but the miracle lies in its intensity, timing, selectivity (firstborn males only), and its avoidance of the Israelites. (Ellicott) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm

---

### v. 30 — The Great Cry in Egypt

- **Traditional Reading:** The “great cry” fulfilled the prophecy of Exodus 11:6. The combination of public calamity, private grief, and shocked religious feeling produced a cry “such as there was none like it.” Coffman suggests the fact that everyone rose in the night indicates the deaths came with violent, painful visitation — victims cried out and aroused their households. (Coffman) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/exodus-12.html
- “There was not a house where there was not one dead” — Coffman treats this as a Hebraic hyperbole, meaning a major proportion of homes, not literally every single house (e.g., those without firstborns). (Coffman)

---

### vv. 31–32 — Pharaoh’s Capitulation and Request for Blessing

- **Traditional Reading:** Pharaoh now *commands* Israel to go — exactly as the LORD had foretold in Exodus 11:1: “he will surely drive you out.” The word “also” in “take your flocks and herds as well” indicates Pharaoh had previously tried to negotiate terms (men only, no livestock, etc.) but now concedes everything. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/
- **“Bless me also”:** This is striking. Pharaoh, who thought himself a god, now asks for blessing from the God of slaves. Guzik says Pharaoh only came to this knowledge through being broken. (Enduring Word)

---

### vv. 33–34 — The Egyptians Urge Israel to Leave / Unleavened Dough

- **Traditional Reading:** The Egyptians feared “we are all going to die,” so they hastened Israel out. The people took their dough before it could rise, carrying kneading bowls wrapped in clothing on their shoulders. This fulfilled the requirement for unleavened bread — but now as a practical necessity, not just a ritual command. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/
- **Application:** Guzik notes that sometimes God arranges circumstances to make obedience unavoidable — even for those who might not have chosen it. (Enduring Word)

---

### vv. 35–36 — The Plundering of the Egyptians

- **Traditional Reading:** Israel “asked” the Egyptians for silver, gold, and clothing, and the LORD “gave the people such favor” that the Egyptians granted everything. This was not theft but a willing transfer born of fear and perhaps guilt. The word “plundered” (or “spoiled”) emphasizes that Israel left not as escaped slaves but as a liberated people carrying the wealth of their former oppressors — a reversal echoing God’s promise to Abraham (Gen 15:14). (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/
- **Prosperity / Word of Faith Note:** Some modern popular teachers cite these verses as proof that God wants believers to claim wealth from unbelievers. While I could not find direct sourcing from the permitted sites on this specific debate, the traditional evangelical reading (as seen on Enduring Word and Precept Austin) treats this as a one-time divinely orchestrated event of justice and provision for the journey ahead, not a universal promise of financial transfer.

---

### v. 37 — From Rameses to Succoth: The 600,000 Men

- **Traditional Reading:** “About 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children.” Multiple commentaries agree that “men” (Hebrew *gëbârim*) means strong, able-bodied men fit for war — those above twenty years of age (cf. Numbers 1:3). This yields a total population estimate of roughly 2 million (some say 2.4 million). (Ellicott; F.B. Meyer; Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/12-37.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/exodus-12.html
- **Rameses:** The starting point, identified with Pi-Ramesu, the capital of the 19th Dynasty pharaohs (likely Rameses II), a suburb of Tanis/Zoan. (Ellicott via biblehub) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/12-37.htm
- **Succoth:** Meaning “booths” or “tents.” Probably a temporary encampment south-east of Tanis. It was the first rallying point where the various bands converged. (Pulpit Commentary; F.B. Meyer) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/12-37.htm
- **Logistical Considerations:** Pulpit Commentary notes the difficulty of 2 million people departing in one day from one place, and suggests that the main body started from Rameses with Moses and Aaron while other groups started from all parts of Goshen and converged on Succoth. The open country and firm soil at that time of year facilitated travel. (Pulpit) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/12-37.htm
- **Modern Scholarly Note:** Some modern scholars question whether the numbers are literal or symbolic, but the classic commentaries treat them as roughly accurate. The NET Bible notes simply present the numbers without demurral. — https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Exo+12%3A40-42

---

### v. 38 — The Mixed Multitude

- **Traditional Reading:** “A mixed multitude” (Hebrew root related to “swarm,” same as the plague of gadflies in Ex 8:21) went up with Israel. These were non-Israelites — Egyptians and possibly other foreigners — who attached themselves to Israel because they saw the God of Israel was greater than Egypt’s gods. (Enduring Word, citing Cole) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/
- These people would later cause problems (cf. Numbers 11:4, where the “rabble” incites complaining).

---

### v. 39 — Unleavened Cakes: Necessity Meets Obedience

- **Traditional Reading:** The Israelites baked unleavened cakes because they were “driven out” and “could not delay.” They had not prepared provisions. This underscores the haste of the departure and shows how God’s ritual command (eat unleavened bread) aligned with practical necessity. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/

---

### vv. 40–41 — The 430 Years, to the Very Day

- **Traditional Reading:** The stay in Egypt lasted 430 years. “To the very day” suggests that the Exodus commenced on the exact anniversary of the day Jacob entered Egypt — a remarkable example of God fulfilling promises on anniversaries. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/
- **Textual Issue:** The Hebrew says “the sojourning of the children of Israel, which dwelt in Egypt” (KJV) or “which they sojourned in Egypt.” The Septuagint (LXX) adds “and in the land of Canaan,” making the 430 years cover the patriarchal sojourn as well — yielding only 215 years in Egypt. The Pulpit Commentary defends the Hebrew text as meaning 430 years *in* Egypt, calling the LXX reading “the mistake of a copyist.” (Pulpit) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/12.htm
- **Pauline Usage (Gal 3:17):** Constable notes that Galatians 3:17 also speaks of 430 years, but probably refers to the span from God’s last reconfirmation of the covenant to Jacob at Beersheba (c. 1875 BC) to the giving of the Law at Sinai (1446 BC). Genesis 15:13 and Acts 7:6 give 400 years for the enslavement period specifically (1846–1446 BC). (Dr. Constable) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-12.html
- **“All the LORD’s divisions”** (or “armies” / “hosts”): Israel is depicted as an army marching out under its divine Commander — a nation born in a day. (Enduring Word; Ellicott)

---

### v. 42 — A Night of Vigil

- **Traditional Reading:** “Because the LORD kept a vigil that night … this same night is to be a vigil to the LORD.” Some Israelites began their march before the night was over, being “hastened” by the Egyptians, though the bulk started at daybreak. The night was “that night of the LORD” — the one for which observances had already been prescribed (vv. 6–11). (Pulpit) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/12.htm
- Guzik calls this the “cross-like event of the Old Testament” — God’s great redemptive act. The phrase “out of Egypt” is repeated 56 times in Scripture after this point. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/

---

### v. 43 — No Foreigner Shall Eat the Passover

- **Traditional Reading:** This supplementary ordinance (vv. 43–49) was likely given to Moses at Succoth. “No foreigner” means no one of a foreign race who wishes to remain uncircumcised and retain a foreign character. This is not ethnic exclusion but covenant exclusion — the door remains open (see v. 48). (Ellicott; Pulpit) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm
- **Catholic Reading:** Haydock notes that the Passover prefigures the Eucharist, which is also to be eaten only by those properly initiated (baptised, in a state of grace). (Haydock) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/exodus-12.html

---

### v. 44 — The Purchased Slave May Eat (After Circumcision)

- **Traditional Reading:** Slaves born in the house were already required to be circumcised on the eighth day (Gen 17:13). Bought slaves were allowed to choose circumcision and thereby gain full religious equality with their master — a remarkable provision for that era. The circumcised slave was admitted to full participation. (Ellicott) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm

---

### v. 45 — Temporary Resident and Hired Hand Excluded

- **Traditional Reading:** A “sojourner” (temporary resident) and a “hired servant” (day labourer) were not permanent members of the covenant household and therefore could not partake. This distinguishes between those who belong to the household through covenant and those merely passing through or employed. (Ellicott; Pulpit) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm

---

### v. 46 — Eaten in One House; No Bone Broken

- **Traditional Reading:** The lamb had to be eaten inside one house — it was a domestic, family-level celebration. None of the meat could be carried outside. (Enduring Word; Ellicott) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/
- **“Nor shall you break any of its bones”:** Two interpretations among older commentators:
  1. *Practical:* Eating in haste left no time to break bones for marrow (Gill; Calvin via Gill). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm
  2. *Typological/Symbolic:* The lamb was roasted whole as a “symbol of unity” — a type of Christ through whom believers are brought into unity with God and each other. The unbroken bones point directly to Christ, whose bones were not broken on the cross (John 19:33–36; Ps 34:20). (Ellicott; Pulpit) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/12.htm
- **Catholic Note:** Haydock ties this directly to the Eucharist: “Here we eat the lamb without breaking a bone, though we take the whole victim.” (Haydock) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/exodus-12.html
- **Justin Martyr (early Church):** Reported that the lamb was prepared on two wooden spits — one vertical, one transverse — forming a cross shape, making it a vivid type of the Crucified One. (Ellicott) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm

---

### v. 47 — Whole Congregation Must Celebrate

- **Traditional Reading:** “All the congregation of Israel shall keep it.” You could not be part of God’s people and not share in Passover. Participation was not optional for the covenant community. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/

---

### vv. 48–49 — The Foreigner Who Wants to Celebrate: Circumcision Required

- **Traditional Reading:** A “foreigner” (stranger) who *wants* to keep Passover must have all males in his household circumcised. Then “he shall be like a native of the land.” This is the path to full inclusion — covenant initiation through circumcision. The same law applies to native-born and foreigner alike — there is one standard. (Enduring Word; Ellicott) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm
- **Typological / Reformed Note (Mackintosh):** Circumcision signifies “the sentence of death written upon nature” — its antitype is the cross. Only those who have accepted the cross (death to the flesh) can “intelligently feed upon Christ.” (Mackintosh) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/nfp/exodus-12.html
- **Baptist / Evangelical (F.B. Meyer):** Circumcision is “the type of putting away the sins of the flesh” (Col 2:11). “We must be separated from sin, before we can claim our portion in the Paschal Lamb.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/exodus-12.html
- **Bridgeway Commentary:** The Israelites were not to lower God’s requirements to suit foreigners; rather, they were to encourage foreigners to carry out covenant requirements and join as worshippers of Yahweh. (Bridgeway) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/exodus-12.html
- **Denominational Note (Covenant Theology / Paedobaptism vs. Credobaptism):** These verses are sometimes discussed in the debate over whether the covenant sign (circumcision / baptism) should be applied to households including infants. I could not locate direct denominational treatment from the permitted sites within my search/fetch limits. The traditional reading consistently sees circumcision as prerequisite for Passover participation, with household inclusion of all males — a pattern that Reformed covenant theologians cite in support of infant baptism, while Baptists note that the foreigner *wanted* to celebrate (profession of faith) before the sign was applied.

---

### v. 50 — Obedience of All Israel

- **Traditional Reading:** “Then all the Israelites did this — they did just as the LORD had commanded.” This mirrors v. 28 and frames the entire section with Israel’s obedience. The response of faith saved their firstborn, plundered the Egyptians, and set them free. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/

---

### v. 51 — Departure “On That Very Day” by Their Divisions

- **Traditional Reading:** “On that very day” — the 15th of Abib (cf. Ex 13:4). Some had started during the night, others in the morning. Ellicott notes this verse would more naturally belong at the start of Exodus 13, with which it is grammatically united. (Ellicott) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm
- **“By their divisions”** (or “armies”): Israel left not as a rabble but as ordered hosts — a nation born in a day. The 430 years of sojourn were like gestation, the plagues like labour pains, and now the nation was born. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/

---

## Summary of Distinctive Traditions (Where Found)

| Topic | View | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Nature of the Tenth Plague** | Angelic agency (“the destroyer”), possibly combined with natural pestilence made miraculous by timing and selectivity | Ellicott (Anglican) |
| **430 Years** | Hebrew text = 430 years *in* Egypt. LXX = 430 including Canaan sojourn. Gal 3:17 harmonised as covenant-to-Law span | Pulpit; Constable (Evangelical) |
| **“No bone broken”** | Type of Christ crucified (Justin Martyr, Ellicott, Catholic); also practical haste (Gill, Calvin) | Ellicott; Gill; Haydock |
| **Passover → Eucharist** | Catholic: The lamb prefigures Christ in the Eucharist, eaten whole without breaking a bone, in the “house” (church) | Haydock (Catholic) |
| **Circumcision prerequisite** | Sentence of death on the flesh (cross) before feeding on Christ — Reformed/ Dispensational (Mackintosh); putting away sins of flesh (F.B. Meyer — Baptist/Holiness) | Mackintosh; F.B. Meyer |
| **Plundering Egyptians** | Traditional evangelical: one-time divine justice and provision, not a universal wealth-transfer promise | Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic) |

*Note: Detailed treatment of modern prosperity/Word of Faith teachings on vv. 35–36, and explicit denominational statements from Lutheran (LCMS), Methodist, or Orthodox sources on these specific verses, were not available within my search limits.*
